items.title: Annie Ross — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When I came from Pittsburgh with my child, we went and stayed with Bird, who was with Chan and Pree, the little girl who died. We all packed into this apartment.

ctx.x: Let’s go ahead and stop now. Annie, if we could go back, for the sake of the chronology. If we could get the full name of your son, and his actual – the year of his birth.

He was born on Christmas Eve. Was it 1950? His full name was Kenneth Christopher Clarke, Christopher being one of Charlie Parker’s names. Bird sent a telegram saying, “I still got lots of other names left.” When I came from Pittsburgh with my child, we went and stayed with Bird, who was with Chan and Pree, the little girl who died. We all packed into this apartment. It was quite wonderful. There were a lot of kids. It was a lot of noise. Again, we had no money. Bird came home with a ham. Boy, a ham. I prepared it…

Klook had impressed on me, time. So when I would get together with he and Moody, it was all about ears. Even when I was in Paris, Moody used to come with Ravel or Debussy. He’d say, listen to that thing that Debussy does [Ross sings], and I could hear the chord change. So Moody was responsible for my enlarging my capacity to hear. It was a fantastic schooling. I remember when I was living in Paris in this hotel, I went to North Africa with Hawk [Coleman Hawkins] and Klook and Moody. That wasn’t bad. Then I did a…

items.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: Well there was Dizzy, there was Bird, you know, there was Clifford Brown

ctx.x: It was a great time. Plus you were making contacts for years to come, right?

Well there was Dizzy, there was Bird, you know, there was Clifford Brown, who didn’t come over there but when I sang with the Hampton band, our trumpet section was Art Farmer, Clifford Brown and Quincy Jones. That’s not too shabby.
Yeah. That was around the early 50s with Hampton?
